claim: Callosal projections from primary somatosensory cortex (S1) are key for processing somatosensory inputs and integrating sensory-motor information.
source: Callosal projections from primary somatosensory cortex (S1) are key for processing somatosensory inputs and integrating sensory-motor information.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about the function of callosal projections.

claim: The normal termination pattern of callosal projections is disrupted in cortex specific NMDAR mutants.
source: We found that the normal termination pattern of these callosal projections is disrupted in cortex specific NMDAR mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing disrupted callosal innervation patterns in NMDAR mutants.

claim: In NMDAR mutants, callosal axons are uniformly distributed throughout S1 rather than projecting selectively to the S1/S2 border.
source: Rather than projecting selectively to the primary/secondary somatosensory cortex (S1/S2) border, axons were uniformly distributed throughout S1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The density of callosal projection in NMDAR mutants increased over postnatal life until the mice died by P30.
source: In addition, the density of this projection increased over postnatal life until the mice died by P30.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative fluorescence density analysis at different time points shown in the manuscript.

claim: GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors in target S1 mediate the callosal guidance phenotype.
source: By combining genetic and antibody-mediated loss of function, we demonstrated that it is GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors in target S1 that mediate this guidance phenotype, thus playing a central role in interhemispheric connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by genetic deletion experiments comparing GluN2A and GluN2B knockout mice, and antibody-mediated loss of function experiments.

claim: The function of NMDA receptors in callosal circuit formation is independent of ion channel function.
source: Furthermore, we found that this function of NMDA receptors in callosal circuit formation is independent of ion channel function and works with the EPHRIN-B/EPHB system.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using MK-801 and D-APV to block NMDAR channel function without affecting callosal innervation patterns.

claim: NMDAR works with the EPHRIN-B/EPHB system in callosal circuit formation.
source: Furthermore, we found that this function of NMDA receptors in callosal circuit formation is independent of ion channel function and works with the EPHRIN-B/EPHB system.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that blocking both NMDAR and EPHRIN-B/EPHB signaling simultaneously is not additive, suggesting they work in the same pathway.

claim: NMDAR in target S1 cortex regulates the formation of callosal circuits by modulating EPH-dependent repulsion.
source: Thus, NMDAR in target S1 cortex regulates the formation callosal circuits perhaps by modulating EPH-dependent repulsion.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings showing interaction between NMDAR and EPHRIN-B/EPHB systems.

claim: The corpus callosum is the largest interhemispheric commissural circuit in mammals.
source: The corpus callosum (CC) is the largest interhemispheric commissural circuit in mammals.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the corpus callosum.

claim: CC connectivity is essential for coordinated sensory-motor function and for many higher cognitive processes.
source: The connectivity of the CC is essential for coordinated sensory-motor function and for many higher cognitive processes, and CC pathology is implicated in a variety of developmental disorders (Paul, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CC pathology is implicated in a variety of developmental disorders.
source: The connectivity of the CC is essential for coordinated sensory-motor function and for many higher cognitive processes, and CC pathology is implicated in a variety of developmental disorders (Paul, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Callosal projections originate from pyramidal neurons located in layers II/III, V, and VI.
source: Callosal projections originate from pyramidal neurons located in layers II/III, V, and VI and traverse the CC to form synapses with neurons in contralateral homotopic or heterotopic cortical areas.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about callosal projections.

claim: Callosal projections traverse the CC to form synapses with neurons in contralateral homotopic or heterotopic cortical areas.
source: Callosal projections originate from pyramidal neurons located in layers II/III, V, and VI and traverse the CC to form synapses with neurons in contralateral homotopic or heterotopic cortical areas.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about callosal projections.

claim: The medial-lateral topography of callosal neurons in the cortex is tightly constrained by the dorsal-ventral position of axons within the CC.
source: We previously showed (Zhou et al., 2013) that the medial-lateral topography of callosal neurons in the cortex is tightly constrained by the dorsal-ventral (D-V) position of axons within the CC.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The axon position within the CC determines its terminal location in the contralateral cortex, with dorsally located axons projecting medially and ventrally located axons projecting laterally.
source: The axon position within the CC determines its terminal location in the contralateral cortex, with dorsally located axons projecting medially and ventrally located axons projecting laterally.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The spatial organization of topographically represented information from one hemisphere is preserved as it is projected onto the contralateral hemisphere.
source: As such, the spatial organization of topographically represented information from one hemisphere is preserved as it is projected onto the contralateral hemisphere.
evidence: This is an inference based on the topographic organization described.

claim: In vivo Ca2+ imaging and multiunit recordings show distinct patterns of neural activity in the cortex of newborn mice.
source: In vivo Ca2+ imaging and multiunit recordings show distinct patterns of neural activity in the cortex of newborn mice (Adelsberger et al., 2005; Khazipov and Luhmann, 2006; Khazipov et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neural activity patterns synchronize spatially and temporally distinct neural networks and may play important roles in wiring cortical maps.
source: These activity patterns synchronize spatially and temporally distinct neural networks and may play important roles in wiring cortical maps (Allène et al., 2008; Golshani et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and includes speculative language ('may play').

claim: Suppressing endogenous neural activity by overexpressing Kir2.1 in callosal neurons delays axon growth and results in layer-targeting defects in visual cortex and somatosensory cortex.
source: Suppressing endogenous neural activity by overexpressing the inward rectifying potassium channel Kir2.1 in callosal neurons delays axon growth and results ultimately in layer-targeting defects in visual cortex and somatosensory cortex (Mizuno et al., 2007; Rodríguez-Tornos et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sensory deprivation by ablating whiskers or transecting the infraorbital nerve before P5 blocks sensory activity to the trigeminal nerve and disrupts barrel field formation in primary somatosensory cortex with secondary disruption of callosal innervation at the S1/S2 border.
source: Sensory deprivation by ablating whiskers or transecting the infraorbital nerve (ION) before P5 blocks sensory activity to the trigeminal nerve and disrupts barrel field formation in primary somatosensory cortex (S1) with secondary disruption of callosal innervation at the S1/S2 border (Huang et al., 2013; Suárez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The NMDA receptor is a glutamatergic neurotransmitter receptor located at the synapses that mediates the vast majority of excitatory neurotransmission in the cortex.
source: The NMDA receptor (NMDAR) is a glutamatergic neurotransmitter receptor located at the synapses that mediates the vast majority of excitatory neurotransmission in the cortex (Traynelis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: NMDAR mediated synaptic transmission is important in generating synchronized activity patterns in immature cortex.
source: NMDAR mediated synaptic transmission is important in generating synchronized activity patterns in immature cortex, suggesting that NMDAR Ca2+ channel may be involved in neural circuit formation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about NMDAR function.

claim: At P5, the callosal axons from S1 had reached the white matter underneath contralateral S1.
source: At postnatal day (P) 5, the callosal axons from S1 had reached the white matter underneath contralateral S1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At P8, the callosal axons were diffusely distributed in contralateral S1.
source: At P8, the callosal axons were diffusely distributed in contralateral S1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1C.

claim: By P12, pruning of excess projections led to a refined innervation pattern with a narrow band limited to the S1/S2 border.
source: By P12, pruning of excess projections led to a refined innervation pattern with a narrow band limited to the S1/S2 border (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: After P12, the callosal innervation pattern is generally stable, as shown at P30.
source: After P12, the pattern is generally stable, as shown at P30 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In P14 control mice (Emx1cre/+; Grin1fl/wt), the callosal innervation pattern of S1 of the contralateral cortex is well differentiated with a dense innervation at S1/S2 border.
source: In P14 control mice (Emx1cre/+; Grin1fl/wt), the callosal innervation pattern of S1 of the contralateral cortex is well differentiated with a dense innervation at S1/S2 border.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In GluN1 KO mice (Emx1cre/+; Grin1fl/fl), the innervation pattern was disrupted and projections were extremely diffused.
source: In GluN1 KO mice (Emx1cre/+; Grin1fl/fl), the innervation pattern was disrupted and projections were extremely diffused which also persisted to P30 (K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1G and 1K.

claim: GluN1 is the essential subunit of NMDARs.
source: The GluN1 subunit is the essential subunit of NMDARs (Dingledine et al., 1999; Paoletti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Global GluN1 knockout mice die within a few hours of birth.
source: Global GluN1 knockout mice die within a few hours of birth (Forrest et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Expression of cortical GluN1 was greatly diminished in GluN1 KO mice at P8.
source: Immunostaining and western blot at P8 showed that expression of cortical GluN1 was greatly diminished (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) in GluN1 KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The organization of thalamocortical barrels in Layer IV of S1 was somewhat disrupted but still apparent in GluN1 KO mice at P8.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Iwasato et al., 2000; Lo et al., 2013), the organization of thalamocortical barrels in Layer IV of S1 was somewhat disrupted but still apparent in GluN1 KO mice at P8, as revealed by vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (VGlut2) immunostaining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by VGlut2 immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: In GluN1 KO mice, the normal restricted pattern of callosal targeting to the S1/S2 border was absent, and callosal axons were uniformly distributed throughout the contralateral somatosensory cortex.
source: However, in GluN1 KO mice (Emx1cre/+; Grin1fl/fl mice), the normal restricted pattern of callosal targeting to the S1/S2 border was absent, and callosal axons were uniformly distributed throughout the contralateral somatosensory cortex (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The axon distribution pattern in S1 was statistically significantly different between littermate control and GluN1 KO mice.
source: Quantitative fluorescence intensity analysis showed that the axon distribution pattern in S1 was statistically significantly different between littermate control and GluN1 KO mice (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative fluorescence intensity analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: GluN1 KO mice had more overall callosal axons innervating S1 at P14.
source: Additionally, fluorescence density analysis showed that GluN1 KO mice also had more overall callosal axons innervating S1 at P14 (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence density analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: In the absence of NMDAR, the targeted callosal innervation of the S1/S2 border was lost, and the overall callosal innervation in S1 was significantly increased.
source: This result suggests that the NMDAR plays a role in callosal circuit formation. In the absence of NMDAR, the targeted callosal innervation of the S1/S2 border was lost, and the overall callosal innervation in S1 was significantly increased.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing disrupted callosal innervation patterns in NMDAR mutants.

claim: GluN1 KO mice were smaller than littermate controls after P5 and rarely survived past P30.
source: GluN1 KO mice were smaller than littermate controls after P5 (data not shown) and rarely survived past P30 so we chose P30 as the last time point to determine if this defect persists.
evidence: This is an experimental observation about the phenotype of GluN1 KO mice.

claim: The callosal innervation phenotype in GluN1 KO mice worsens after P14.
source: We found that this phenotype worsens after P14 (Figure 1J–L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1J-L.

claim: GluN1 KO mice showed no differences with littermate controls at P0, P3, and P5.
source: GluN1 KO mice showed no differences with littermate controls at P0, P3, and P5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) indicating no difference in the overall rate of axon growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: GluN1 KO mice showed earlier and increased innervation of S1 at P6, when callosal axons start entering the contralateral cortex.
source: However, GluN1 KO mice showed earlier and increased innervation of S1 at P6, when callosal axons start entering the contralateral cortex (Figure 2B and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B and E.

claim: In control littermates at P6, callosal axons were gathered into a bundle under contralateral S1 with few axons penetrating into S1.
source: In control littermates, at P6, callosal axons were gathered into a bundle under contralateral S1 with few axons penetrating into S1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In GluN1 KO mice at P6, axons targeting S1 had extended past layer V, with many axons terminating in layer II/III.
source: In contrast, axons targeting S1 in GluN1 KO mice at P6 had extended past layer V, with many axons terminating in layer II/III (arrows in S1 in Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Control mice showed equal degrees of callosal innervation from medial to lateral S1 at P6.
source: Interestingly, while control mice showed equal degrees of callosal innervation from medial to lateral S1 (see arrows in S1 in Figure 2A), GluN1 KO mice showed preferential early callosal innervation of medial S1 (see arrows in S1 in Figure 2B), and this was even more apparent at P8 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GluN1 KO mice showed preferential early callosal innervation of medial S1 at P6.
source: Interestingly, while control mice showed equal degrees of callosal innervation from medial to lateral S1 (see arrows in S1 in Figure 2A), GluN1 KO mice showed preferential early callosal innervation of medial S1 (see arrows in S1 in Figure 2B), and this was even more apparent at P8 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In control mice, cleaved caspase-3+ cells were mostly detected in layer II/III of primary motor cortex (M1), and rarely were observed in other cortical regions.
source: In control mice, cleaved caspase-3+ cells were mostly detected in layer II/III of primary motor cortex (M1), and rarely were observed in other cortical regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by cleaved caspase-3 immunostaining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: GluN1 KO mutants had increased cell death in layer II/III of M1.
source: Mutants did have increased cell death in layer II/III of M1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B'); however, there was no increase in cell death in other cortical regions including S1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B'').
evidence: This is supported by cleaved caspase-3 immunostaining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B'.

claim: There was no increase in cell death in S1 of GluN1 KO mutants.
source: Mutants did have increased cell death in layer II/III of M1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B'); however, there was no increase in cell death in other cortical regions including S1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B'').
evidence: This is supported by cleaved caspase-3 immunostaining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B''.

claim: The deletion of NMDAR in excitatory cortical neurons leads to premature and disrupted callosal innervation of contralateral S1.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the deletion of NMDAR in excitatory cortical neurons leads to premature and disrupted callosal innervation of contralateral S1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing earlier and increased callosal innervation in NMDAR mutants.

claim: The excessive callosal innervation in NMDAR mutants persists and is not corrected by pruning of mistargeted axons at later developmental stages.
source: Furthermore, this excessive innervation persists and is not corrected by pruning of mistargeted axons at later developmental stages.
evidence: This is based on observations that the phenotype continues to worsen after P14.

claim: Presynaptic deletion of GluN1 from neurons had no discernible effect on callosal innervation at P14.
source: Compared with littermate controls (Figure 3B), presynaptic deletion of GluN1 (ipsiS1-/-) from neurons had no discernible effect on callosal innervation at P14 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: NMDAR is not required for projecting neurons to properly target S1.
source: This suggests that NMDAR is not required for projecting neurons to properly target S1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that presynaptic deletion of GluN1 had no effect on callosal innervation.

claim: Selective deletion of postsynaptic GluN1 strikingly increased callosal S1 innervation.
source: However, selective deletion of postsynaptic GluN1 in experimental mice strikingly increased callosal S1 innervation (Figure 3G and H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) similar to the deletion of GluN1 in all excitatory cortical neurons (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3G, 3H, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: NMDAR is required in the target neurons only for normal callosal circuit formation.
source: These results suggest that NMDAR is required in the target neurons only for normal callosal circuit formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that postsynaptic but not presynaptic deletion of GluN1 disrupts callosal innervation.

claim: Anti-NMDAR antibodies directed to an extracellular domain of GluN1 downregulate the numbers of surface NMDARs.
source: NMDAR antibodies directed to an extracellular domain of GluN1 are known to downregulate the numbers of surface NMDARs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the effects of anti-NMDAR antibodies.

claim: The anti-GluN1 antibody can alter the surface distribution and dynamics of NMDAR.
source: It has been shown that this antibody can alter the surface distribution and dynamics of NMDAR (Dupuis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The distribution of anti-GluN1 antibodies was most abundant in deep cortical layers of the ipsilateral injected hemisphere.
source: The distribution of anti-GluN1 antibodies was most abundant in deep cortical layers of the ipsilateral injected hemisphere (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Contralateral but not ipsilateral antibody injections led to more overall callosal innervation in S1 at P14.
source: The fluorescence density analysis at P14 showed that the contralateral (Figure 4E–H) but not ipsilateral antibody injections (Figure 4A–D) led to more overall callosal innervation in S1 at P14.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence density analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Contralateral/target expression of NMDAR in deep cortical layers is required for callosal axon targeting.
source: This further supports our genetic data that contralateral/target expression of NMDAR in deep cortical layers is required for callosal axon targeting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the antibody injection experiments showing that contralateral but not ipsilateral injections affect callosal innervation.

claim: Antibody injections from P4 to P8 had increased callosal axonal growth into S1 similar to that observed in NMDAR genetic deletion mice.
source: We found that antibody injections from P4 to P8 had increased callosal axonal growth into S1 similar to that observed in NMDAR genetic deletion mice (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Antibody injections only from P8 to P14 had no effect on the overall callosal innervation pattern.
source: However, antibody injections only from P8 to P14 had no effect on the overall callosal innervation pattern and we saw no increased callosal innervation in S1 (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: The crucial effect of NMDAR on callosal circuit formation is primarily during callosal projection into the cortex (P6–P8).
source: Thus, taking the genetic and antibody injection data together suggests that the crucial effect of NMDAR on callosal circuit formation is primarily during callosal projection into the cortex (P6–P8).
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal specificity of the antibody injection effects.

claim: GluN2A- and GluN2B-containing NMDARs are functionally distinct.
source: GluN2A- and GluN2B-containing NMDARs are functionally distinct (Kutsuwada et al., 1992; Loftis and Janowsky, 2003) and follow different developmental expression trajectories with GluN2B as the major NR2 subunit during the first postnatal week and GluN2A expression present but increasing thereafter (Liu et al., 2004; Monyer et al., 1994; Sans et al., 2000; Sheng et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GluN2B is the major NR2 subunit during the first postnatal week and GluN2A expression is present but increasing thereafter.
source: GluN2A- and GluN2B-containing NMDARs are functionally distinct (Kutsuwada et al., 1992; Loftis and Janowsky, 2003) and follow different developmental expression trajectories with GluN2B as the major NR2 subunit during the first postnatal week and GluN2A expression present but increasing thereafter (Liu et al., 2004; Monyer et al., 1994; Sans et al., 2000; Sheng et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GluN2A was dramatically diminished in Emx1cre/+; Grin2afl/fl mice at P8.
source: To address previous studies that found that GluN2A was expressed at lower levels during development, we checked the expression of GluN2A in S1 at P8 and found that it was dramatically diminished in Emx1cre/+; Grin2afl/fl mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B), while the expression of GluN2B was the same in control and Emx1cre/+; Grin2afl/fl mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and C), and similarly GluN2A expression was unchanged in Emx1cre/+; Grin2bfl/fl mice (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The expression of GluN2B was the same in control and Emx1cre/+; Grin2afl/fl mice.
source: To address previous studies that found that GluN2A was expressed at lower levels during development, we checked the expression of GluN2A in S1 at P8 and found that it was dramatically diminished in Emx1cre/+; Grin2afl/fl mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B), while the expression of GluN2B was the same in control and Emx1cre/+; Grin2afl/fl mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and C), and similarly GluN2A expression was unchanged in Emx1cre/+; Grin2bfl/fl mice (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and C.

claim: In GluN2A KO mice, the overall callosal innervation pattern was similar to control mice, although there was increased callosal innervation at the M1/S1 border at P14.
source: In GluN2A KO mice, the overall callosal innervation pattern was similar to control mice, although there was increased callosal innervation at the M1/S1 border at P14 (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: GluN2B deletion phenocopied GluN1 deletion with increased S1 innervation and loss of targeted innervation of the S1/S2 border at P14.
source: In contrast, GluN2B deletion phenocopied GluN1 deletion with increased S1 innervation and loss of targeted innervation of the S1/S2 border at P14 (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: GluN2B KO mice were smaller than littermate controls after P5 and rarely survived past P30.
source: Similar to GluN1 KO mice, GluN2B KO mice were smaller than littermate controls after P5 and rarely survived past P30.
evidence: This is an experimental observation about the phenotype of GluN2B KO mice.

claim: Either GluN2A-containing or GluN2B-containing NMDAR is channel competent.
source: Either GluN2A-containing or GluN2B-containing NMDAR is channel competent and GluN2A-containing NMDARs are present in the cortex of GluN2B KO mice, thus it seems possible that NMDAR's role in callosal circuit development may be separable from its channel activity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about NMDAR subunit composition and function.

claim: NMDAR's role in callosal circuit development may be separable from its channel activity.
source: Either GluN2A-containing or GluN2B-containing NMDAR is channel competent and GluN2A-containing NMDARs are present in the cortex of GluN2B KO mice, thus it seems possible that NMDAR's role in callosal circuit development may be separable from its channel activity.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that GluN2B deletion causes a phenotype despite the presence of channel-competent GluN2A-containing NMDARs.

claim: Ca2+ influx through NMDARs is essential for synaptogenesis, experience-dependent synaptic remodeling, and long-lasting changes in synaptic efficacy such as LTP and LTD.
source: Ca2+ influx through NMDARs is essential for synaptogenesis, experience-dependent synaptic remodeling, and long-lasting changes in synaptic efficacy such as long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD) (Collingridge et al., 2004; Lau and Zukin, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: There are NMDAR functions independent of its ion-influx.
source: However, accumulating evidence shows that there are NMDAR functions independent of its ion-influx (Kessels et al., 2013; Nabavi et al., 2013), such as a use-dependent tyrosine dephosphorylation of NMDA receptors is independent of ion flux (Vissel et al., 2001), and NMDAR-dependent LTD which can be induced independent of Ca2+ influx (Dore et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In models of ischemic stroke, neuronal death caused by overactivation of NMDAR is independent of Ca2+ influx, but dependent on signaling complexes formed by NMDARs, Src kinase, and Panx1.
source: In models of ischemic stroke, neuronal death caused by overactivation of NMDAR is also independent of Ca2+ influx, but dependent on signaling complexes formed by NMDARs, Src kinase, and Panx1 (Weilinger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: MK-801 is a non-competitive NMDAR antagonist that enters the open NMDAR channel and binds to the 'blocking site' located deep in the pore, blocking Ca2+ influx through NMDAR.
source: MK-801 enters the open NMDAR channel and binds to the 'blocking site' located deep in the pore, blocking Ca2+ influx through NMDAR (Huettner and Bean, 1988, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and represents established knowledge about MK-801 mechanism of action.

claim: Blocking NMDAR with a daily dose of 0.4 mg/kg MK-801 in ferret pups between P14 and P21 disrupted axonal pattern formation by retinal afferents in the lateral geniculate nucleus.
source: Previous studies showed that blocking NMDAR with a daily dose of 0.4 mg/kg MK-801 in ferret pups between P14 and P21 disrupted axonal pattern formation by retinal afferents in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) (Hahm et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: MK801-treated pups gained weight slowly and developed opisthotonic posturing of limbs and head, suggesting the channel function of NMDAR had been blocked.
source: Compared with saline control, MK801-treated pups gained weight slowly and developed opisthotonic posturing of limbs and head (data not shown), suggesting the channel function of NMDAR had been blocked.
evidence: This is an experimental observation and inference about the effectiveness of MK-801 treatment.

claim: The normal callosal innervation pattern in MK-801 treated pups was similar to saline-treated controls.
source: However, the normal callosal innervation pattern in these pups was similar to saline-treated controls (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: D-APV competitively blocks the ligand (glutamate) binding site to NMDAR and inhibits channel opening, thereby preventing Ca2+ influx.
source: We also performed similar experiments using D(-)−2-amino-5-phosphonopentanoic acid (D-APV), which competitively blocks the ligand (glutamate) binding site to NMDAR and inhibits channel opening, thereby preventing Ca2+ influx (Morris, 1989, Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and represents established knowledge about D-APV mechanism of action.

claim: D-APV-treated pups developed unilateral muscle contractions in limbs on the opposite side of the injection, suggesting the channel function of NMDAR had been blocked.
source: Compared with saline control, D-APV-treated pups developed unilateral muscle contractions in limbs on the opposite side of the injection (data not shown), suggesting the channel function of NMDAR had been blocked.
evidence: This is an experimental observation and inference about the effectiveness of D-APV treatment.

claim: The callosal innervation pattern in D-APV treated pups was similar to saline controls.
source: However, the callosal innervation pattern in these pups was again similar to saline controls (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 7F-H.

claim: NMDAR function in callosal targeting is independent of its channel activity.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that NMDAR function in callosal targeting is independent of its channel activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blocking NMDAR channel activity with MK-801 or D-APV does not affect callosal innervation patterns.

claim: NMDAR subunits bind directly to EPHB axon guidance receptors.
source: Previous studies have shown that NMDAR subunits bind directly to EPHB axon guidance receptors (Dalva et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: EPHB receptor tyrosine kinases and their transmembrane-ligands, the EPHRIN-B family, mediate short-distance cell–cell signaling and regulate many developmental processes including ordered neural maps.
source: EPHB receptor tyrosine kinases and their transmembrane-ligands, the EPHRIN-B family, mediate short-distance cell–cell signaling and thus regulate many developmental processes at the interface between pattern formation and morphogenesis, including ordered neural maps (Kania and Klein, 2016; Niethamer and Bush, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: EPHRIN-B1 and EPHB2 are involved in earlier stages of CC midline axon crossing.
source: Further, several members of the EPH/EPHRIN family, including EPHRIN-B1 and EPHB2, are involved in earlier stages of CC midline axon crossing, strengthening their relevance in this context (Bush and Soriano, 2009; Orioli et al., 1996; Robichaux et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EPHB2 and NMDARs colocalize at postsynaptic dendrites.
source: EPHB2 and NMDARs colocalize at postsynaptic dendrites, and the extracellular domain of NMDAR interacts directly with EPHB2, an interaction driven by activation of EPHB2 by clustered EPHRIN-B1 expressed in presynaptic axon terminals (Dalva et al., 2000; Nolt et al., 2011; Palmer and Klein, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The extracellular domain of NMDAR interacts directly with EPHB2, an interaction driven by activation of EPHB2 by clustered EPHRIN-B1 expressed in presynaptic axon terminals.
source: EPHB2 and NMDARs colocalize at postsynaptic dendrites, and the extracellular domain of NMDAR interacts directly with EPHB2, an interaction driven by activation of EPHB2 by clustered EPHRIN-B1 expressed in presynaptic axon terminals (Dalva et al., 2000; Nolt et al., 2011; Palmer and Klein, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mice lacking EPHB2 have reduced levels of NMDARs at synapses in the hippocampus and cortex.
source: Mice lacking EPHB2 have reduced levels of NMDARs at synapses in the hippocampus and cortex (Henkemeyer et al., 2003; Sheffler-Collins and Dalva, 2012), suggesting coordinated localization.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EPHB2 preferentially decreases Ca2+-dependent inactivation of GluN2B-containing NMDARs but not GluN2A-containing NMDARs at synapses of mature neurons.
source: EPHB2 also preferentially decreases Ca2+-dependent inactivation of GluN2B-containing NMDARs but not GluN2A-containing NMDARs at synapses of mature neurons (Nolt et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: EPHB2 signaling leads to phosphorylation of GluN2B at tyrosine residue 1472 preventing clathrin-dependent endocytosis, and increasing the surface retention of GluN2B-containing NMDARs.
source: In addition, EPHB2 signaling leads to phosphorylation of GluN2B at tyrosine residue 1472 preventing clathrin-dependent endocytosis, and increasing the surface retention of GluN2B-containing NMDARs (Chen and Roche, 2007; Nolt et al., 2011; Takasu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At P5, EPHB2 was found in both cortex and CC of controls.
source: At P5, EPHB2 was found in both cortex and CC of controls (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In GluN1 KO mice, EPHB2 expression in the cortex was reduced.
source: However, in GluN1 KO mice, EPHB2 expression in the cortex was reduced (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Protein levels of EPHB2 were reduced at least 30% in GluN1 KO mice.
source: Western blots also confirmed that protein levels of EPHB2 were reduced at least 30% in GluN1 KO mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–E) while mRNA levels of EPHB2 were unchanged (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: mRNA levels of EPHB2 were unchanged in GluN1 KO mice.
source: Western blots also confirmed that protein levels of EPHB2 were reduced at least 30% in GluN1 KO mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–E) while mRNA levels of EPHB2 were unchanged (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The punctate staining of EPHB2 on cell membranes was completely lost in red (recombined) cells of Emx1cre/+; Grin1fl/fl; Rosa26fs-tdTomato brain sections.
source: Supporting our hypothesis that loss of GluN1 leads to loss of EPHB2, the punctate staining of EPHB2 on cell membranes was completely lost in red (recombined) cells of Emx1cre/+; Grin1fl/fl; Rosa26fs-tdTomato brain sections but not red cells of Emx1cre/+; Grin1wt/wt; Rosa26fs-tdTomato brain sections (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of NMDAR caused the loss of EPHB2 selectively on cells that lack GluN1 after excision.
source: Taken together, we demonstrated that the loss of NMDAR caused the loss of EPHB2 selectively on cells that lack GluN1 after excision, thus explaining the 30% reduction in EPHB2 protein expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunostaining data showing loss of EPHB2 in GluN1-deleted cells.

claim: When NMDARs are lost, membrane based EPHB2 protein expression in target neurons is lost as well.
source: Because EPHB2 is necessary for localization of NMDAR to postsynaptic terminals, we wondered if this requirement was reciprocal and found indeed that it is – when NMDARs are lost, membrane based EPHB2 protein expression in target neurons is lost as well (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: NMDAR reciprocally regulates the localization of EPHB2.
source: This result suggests that NMDAR reciprocally regulates the localization of EPHB2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that loss of NMDAR leads to loss of EPHB2.

claim: In projecting neurons lacking EPHRIN-B1, callosal axons extended into the cortex past layer V, and many axons terminated in layer II/III, similar to that observed in GluN1 KO mice at P6.
source: In projecting neurons lacking EPHRIN-B1, callosal axons extended into the cortex past layer V, and many axons terminated in layer II/III (arrows in Figure 8C), similar to that observed in GluN1 KO mice at P6 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Unclustered soluble EPHRINs bind EPH receptors but act as antagonists.
source: EPHRINs have to be clustered in a cell membrane or artificially with, for example, antibodies to efficiently activate EPH receptors (Davis et al., 1994). Unclustered soluble EPHRINs bind EPH receptors but act as antagonists (Vearing and Lackmann, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Contralateral injection of soluble EPHRIN-B1-Fc led to increased callosal innervation at P6 with axons penetrating to superficial layers.
source: Compared with littermate controls, contralateral injection of soluble EPHRIN-B1-Fc led to increased callosal innervation at P6 with axons penetrating to superficial layers (Figure 8F, G, and J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8F, G, and J.

claim: EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 play important roles in controlling callosal axon penetration into the contralateral S1 cortex.
source: These results support the idea that EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 play important roles in controlling callosal axon penetration into the contralateral S1 cortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing that blocking EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 signaling increases callosal innervation.

claim: Contralateral injection of anti-GluN1 antibodies caused increased callosal innervation at P6 and penetration to superficial layers of cortex.
source: Compared with controls, contralateral injection of anti-GluN1 antibodies caused increased callosal innervation at P6 and penetration to superficial layers of cortex (Figure 8D, E, and J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8D, E, and J.

claim: Blocking NMDAR and EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 signaling simultaneously in contralateral cortex did not show any additive or synergistic effects.
source: Critically, blocking NMDAR and EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 signaling simultaneously in contralateral cortex by injecting both anti-GluN1 antibody and EPHRIN-B1-Fc did not show any additive or synergistic effects (Figure 8H–J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8H-J.

claim: NMDAR and EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 are in the same pathway in regulating callosal targeting in S1.
source: This suggests that in fact NMDAR and EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 are in the same pathway in regulating callosal targeting in S1 and is consistent with our other findings.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blocking both systems simultaneously is not additive.

claim: NMDARs cooperate with EPHRIN-B/EPHB in controlling callosal circuit formation.
source: In this study, we found that NMDARs cooperate with EPHRIN-B/EPHB in controlling callosal circuit formation and demonstrated that it is GluN2B-containing NMDARs in target S1 cortex that regulate callosal axon targeting in S1.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: In mutants where either GluN2B or GluN1 are disrupted, there is excess axonal growth throughout S1.
source: In mutants where either GluN2B or GluN1 are disrupted, there is excess axonal growth throughout S1.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: This phenotype is most consistent with a loss of a repellant activity that normally restricts commissural axonal projections to the S1 cortex at initial stages of this process.
source: We believe this phenotype is most consistent with a loss of a repellant activity that normally restricts commissural axonal projections to the S1 cortex at initial stages of this process (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The complementary expression of Sema3A and Nrp1 contributes to axonal order within the CC.
source: The complementary expression of chemotropic guidance cue Semaphorin3A (Sem3A) and its receptor Neuropilin-1 (Nrp1) contributes to this axonal order within the CC.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Sema3A/Nrp1 signaling contributes to the topographic order of axons within the CC but is not involved in the axon position-dependent projection to the contralateral target cortex.
source: The studies of genetic manipulations showed that Sema3A/Nrp1 signaling contributes to the topographic order of axons within the CC but is not involved in the axon position-dependent projection to the contralateral target cortex.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Contralateral/target expression of NMDAR controls the pattern of callosal projections to contralateral target S1.
source: Here, in this study, we demonstrated that contralateral/target expression of NMDAR controls the pattern of callosal projections to contralateral target S1.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Despite the disruption of targeting within S1 in mice with disrupted NMDAR, there is little evidence of ectopic projection to other cortical areas.
source: Interestingly, despite the disruption of targeting within S1 in mice with disrupted NMDAR, there is little evidence of ectopic projection to other cortical areas.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: There are other cues that regulate the generic projection to S1 but the mechanisms uncovered help govern the distribution of these axons within S1.
source: This indicates that there are still other cues that regulate the generic projection to S1 but that the mechanisms we have uncovered help govern the distribution of these axons within S1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that axons still project to S1 but are distributed abnormally within it.

claim: NMDAR protein complexes containing GluN1 and GluN2B are critical for commissural projection.
source: These data are consistent with the idea that NMDAR protein complexes containing GluN1 and GluN2B are critical for commissural projection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings showing that both GluN1 and GluN2B deletion cause similar phenotypes.

claim: Without NMDAR containing GluN1 and GluN2B in the target cortex, there is earlier and increased callosal innervation of S1 starting at P6.
source: Our findings suggest that without NMDAR containing GluN1 and GluN2B in the target cortex, there is earlier and increased callosal innervation of S1 starting at P6, when callosal axons start entering the contralateral cortex.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Loss of NMDAR leads to loss of a repellant activity in the cortex that normally limits axon growth into superficial layers of S1, until axons reach the S1/S2 border.
source: We believe that this observation indicates that either loss of NMDAR leads to an increase in the attractiveness of S1 cortex or that loss of NMDAR leads to loss of a repellant activity in the cortex that normally limits axon growth into superficial layers of S1, until axons reach the S1/S2 border.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: EPHRIN-B/EPHB signals are well-known repulsive axon guidance cues.
source: EPHRIN-B/EPHB signals are well-known repulsive axon guidance cues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EPHRIN-B/EPHB signaling.

claim: EPHB2 is necessary for localization of NMDAR to postsynaptic terminals.
source: Because EPHB2 is necessary for localization of NMDAR to postsynaptic terminals, we wondered if this requirement was reciprocal and found indeed that it is – when NMDARs are lost, membrane based EPHB2 protein expression in target neurons is lost as well (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and supported by the experimental findings.

claim: The NMDAR interaction with EPHB2 is driven by the stimulation of EPHB2 by clustered EPHRIN-B1 expressed in presynaptic axon terminals.
source: In addition, the NMDAR interaction with EPHB2 is driven by the stimulation of EPHB2 by clustered EPHRIN-B1 expressed in presynaptic axon terminals, indicating that the interaction may regulate axon guidance and termination.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous literature.

claim: Deletion of EPHRIN-B1 only in projecting callosal axons led to excess ingrowth into the S1 cortex visible from P6 to P8.
source: When we deleted EPHRIN-B1 only in projecting callosal axons, this also led to excess ingrowth into the S1 cortex visible from P6 to P8.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The EPHRIN-B1 deletion phenotype is less severe than the NMDAR phenotype, most likely due to redundancy with other EPHRIN-B ligands also expressed in projecting axons.
source: That this phenotype is less severe than the NMDAR phenotype is most likely due to redundancy with other EPHRIN-B ligands also expressed in projecting axons.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference in phenotype severity.

claim: Injection of EPHRIN-B1-Fc fragments disrupted the somatosensory callosal targeting as efficiently as anti-NMDAR antibodies.
source: To globally disrupt EPHB-EPHRIN-B interactions we injected EPHRIN-B1-Fc fragments and found that these also disrupted the somatosensory callosal targeting as efficiently as anti-NMDAR antibodies; furthermore, these two treatments were neither additive nor synergistic, implying they act through a common pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: EPHRIN-B1-Fc and anti-NMDAR antibody treatments were neither additive nor synergistic, implying they act through a common pathway.
source: To globally disrupt EPHB-EPHRIN-B interactions we injected EPHRIN-B1-Fc fragments and found that these also disrupted the somatosensory callosal targeting as efficiently as anti-NMDAR antibodies; furthermore, these two treatments were neither additive nor synergistic, implying they act through a common pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The production of transient, exuberant axons, and axonal branches is a general phenomenon in development across species and systems.
source: The production of transient, exuberant axons, and axonal branches is a general phenomenon in development across species and systems (De León Reyes et al., 2019; Fenlon et al., 2017; Hand et al., 2015; Innocenti, 2020; Innocenti and Price, 2005; Luo and O'Leary, 2005; Ribeiro Gomes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: NMDAR are required to collaborate with EPHRIN-B/EPHB in target cortex, acting as a repellant to limit early growth of callosal axons into S1 cortex.
source: Our data indicate that NMDAR are required to collaborate with EPHRIN-B/EPHB in target cortex, and the most parsimonious conclusion is that this acts as a repellant to limit early growth of callosal axons into S1 cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: By P30, there is a nearly sixfold increase in axonal extension into S1 in NMDAR mutants.
source: These phenotypes are seen first at P6 when axons inappropriately enter superficial cortex in S1 so that by P30 (when the animals die) there is a nearly sixfold increase in axonal extension into S1.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of the experimental data.

claim: NMDAR plays a role in controlling initial projection into S1 and also later regulating refinement of inappropriate projections by pruning.
source: This is consistent with a role for NMDAR in controlling initial projection into S1 but probably also later regulating refinement of these inappropriate projections by pruning – both core functions of axonal repellants.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Correlated neural activity influences axon branch dynamics of retinal axons in the optic tectum.
source: In vivo time-lapse images of retinal axons from albino Xenopus tadpoles show that correlated neural activity influences axon branch dynamics of retinal axons in the optic tectum (Ruthazer et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Axon branches whose activity is not correlated with that of their neighbors are selectively eliminated.
source: The axon branches whose activity is not correlated with that of their neighbors are selectively eliminated.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Selective elimination of uncorrelated axon branches can be abolished by blocking the Ca2+ influx of NMDAR by MK-801.
source: However, the selective elimination can be abolished by blocking the Ca2+ influx of NMDAR by its antagonist MK-801.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: When Ca2+ influx of NMDAR was blocked by MK-801 or D-APV, there were some subtle, local laminar-specific innervation differences at the S1/S2 border.
source: When we blocked the Ca2+ influx of NMDAR by MK-801 or D-APV, even though the overall callosal innervation pattern of somatosensory cortex was not affected, there were some subtle, local laminar-specific innervation differences at the S1/S2 border, suggesting that the refinement of axon arborization may rely on the Ca2+ influx-mediated activity changes through NMDAR.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The refinement of axon arborization may rely on the Ca2+ influx-mediated activity changes through NMDAR.
source: When we blocked the Ca2+ influx of NMDAR by MK-801 or D-APV, even though the overall callosal innervation pattern of somatosensory cortex was not affected, there were some subtle, local laminar-specific innervation differences at the S1/S2 border, suggesting that the refinement of axon arborization may rely on the Ca2+ influx-mediated activity changes through NMDAR.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: EPHRIN-B/EPHB signaling was previously shown to be involved in infrapyramidal bundle pruning in dentate gyrus.
source: Regarding previous roles of EPHRIN-B/EPHB signaling in pruning, this pathway was previously shown to be involved in infrapyramidal bundle pruning in dentate gyrus (Xu and Henkemeyer, 2009) and it is known that activation of EPHB by EPHRIN-B potentiates Ca2+ influx of NMDA receptor (Takasu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Activation of EPHB by EPHRIN-B potentiates Ca2+ influx of NMDA receptor.
source: Regarding previous roles of EPHRIN-B/EPHB signaling in pruning, this pathway was previously shown to be involved in infrapyramidal bundle pruning in dentate gyrus (Xu and Henkemeyer, 2009) and it is known that activation of EPHB by EPHRIN-B potentiates Ca2+ influx of NMDA receptor (Takasu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: NMDAR and EPHRIN-B/EPHB signaling may cooperate in the refinement of the callosal innervation pattern and perhaps in other circuits.
source: These lines of evidence suggest that NMDAR and EPHRIN-B/EPHB signaling may cooperate in the refinement of the callosal innervation pattern and perhaps in other circuits.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings and previous literature.
